newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi, Florida push ahead with tobacco suits. [CORRECTED 03:45 GMT 25/6]
newsitem.headline: Mississippi, Florida push ahead with tobacco suits. [CORRECTED 03:45 GMT 25/6]

text.p: Mississippi and Florida officials said on Tuesday they were prepared to go ahead with trials of their suits against the tobacco industry in the next two months despite a proposed national settlement.
Mississippi and Florida were among the first states to sue the tobacco industry to recover the costs of treating ill smokers. They have trials scheduled to start on July 7 and Aug. 4, respectively.
Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, who in May 1994 became the first state legal officer to sue, said he was prepared to go ahead with his state's trial unless a settlement was reached.
"They have two options -- the industry -- at this point. They either settle my case or we try," Moore told reporters at a meeting of state attorneys general at Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming.
Any settlement of the Mississippi case would be separate from the proposed nationwide settlement with the tobacco industry announced by state attorneys general last Friday.

That $368.5 billion settlement is designed to end 40 state lawsuits, but it needs congressional action, which could take months. The settlement would force the tobacco industry to sharply reduce the advertising and marketing of cigarettes.

Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth said on Tuesday his state was also going ahead with preparations to try its suit. He denied a published report that it was negotiating with the tobacco industry to delay the trial.

"We're not going to delay our trial, no way. ... I spoke to my governor last night, and I'm meeting him tomorrow, and we're talking about trial strategy. We're ready to go to trial," Butterworth told Reuters.

Moore, who led the national talks, said he planned to meet with tobacco industry representatives on the Mississippi case later this week. He would not say where the talks would be held or give any hint of what he would seek in a settlement.
"I'm going to go negotiate with the industry about Mississippi now. I didn't feel comfortable doing that until this negotiation was done because I was leading the negotiations," he said.
"But because my trial date comes up, I can't afford to move my trial date. I think it would do a disservice to the people I represent. I don't want to be behind all those big states," Moore said.
Moore acknowledged there was a risk the whole agreement could fall apart if he went to trial or the tobacco industry could win and decide it wanted to try other state suits.
"That's obviously a very interesting dynamic that's going to unfold in the next few days. I can't tell you what the resolution of it is going to be," he said.
State attorneys general attending the summer meeting of the National Asssociation of Attorneys General held a second meeting on Tuesday to discuss the proposed tobacco settlement.
Moore said he had asked the attorneys general, whose meeting ends on Thursday, to contact members of Congress and the White House to lobby for the proposed settlement.

Indiana Attorney General Jeffrey Modisett said the officials discussed proposals to divide up the states' share of the tobacco proceeds. An initial proposal to the group on Monday was based on states' spending on treating smoking-related illnesses compared with national spending.

"They made a number of good suggestions that my staff and committee are going to go back and work on, but we think we are headed in the right direction, and we'll probly have a follow-up conference call as early as next week," Modisett said.
The attorneys general did not release any figures and reached no final agreement.
California Attorney General Dan Lungren said the legal officials were "going to look as to how the different formulas affect their states." "That's natural," he added.
"The thing I liked is there was no general griping that this state or that state was not going to be treated fairly," Lungren said. (corrects attribution)
